note: The company half of a wave brief. It exists because a pilot proved it had to: six worlds drawn against six different aesthetic assignments produced six genuinely unrelated surfaces and six nearly identical companies. Every one was hardware-attached measurement with an offline or regulatory constraint, two of them Rotterdam firms shipping lab instruments. The cause was the prompt, which asked for a hard constraint and then listed examples (regulated, offline-first, hardware-attached), so the examples became the answer. A generator supplied with examples will return those examples, which is the same argmax the aesthetic draw exists to break. So the company is drawn too, from enumerated values, and the wave never sees a list of suggestions. Values are drawn uniformly: unlike the aesthetic axes there is no occupancy to weight against, because the catalog records worlds rather than the companies they were designed for.

axes.label: Sector
axes.note: Deliberately wide and deliberately not instrument-heavy, which is the bias the pilot exposed. If a wave starts producing one kind of company again, look here first.

axes.label: Stage and size
values: two founders, pre-revenue, no product yet
forty people, growing fast and breaking things
a century old, family owned, fourth generation
a cooperative owned by its members
a two-person team inside a much larger parent
in managed decline, maintaining a legacy product

axes.label: Who reads the docs
axes.note: The reader shapes the surface more than the sector does. A regulator and a hobbyist want opposite pages from the same company.
values: a customer who did not want to be here and wants to leave
an integration engineer at a partner company
a volunteer with no training and no time
a rival evaluating whether to copy this
an internal team member on their second day
a hobbyist doing this for love at 2am
a procurement officer comparing three vendors
a support agent with the customer on the line
someone's parent, following instructions over the phone

axes.label: The hard constraint
axes.note: Deliberately mixed: commercial, social and temporal constraints alongside technical ones. The pilot's prompt listed only technical constraints and got only technical companies.
values: the business is entirely seasonal, dead for eight months
two sided marketplace, neither side trusts the other
the product is legally required and nobody wants it
sold through franchises the company does not control
the audience does not read the company's language
most usage happens with no network
the product can kill someone if it is wrong
the company competes against a free government service
revenue comes from advertisers, not from readers
the thing being documented changes weekly
the thing being documented has not changed in thirty years
users are anonymous by design and cannot be contacted
the buyer and the user are different people who disagree
adoption depends on a community that distrusts the company

axes.label: The documentation surface
axes.note: Docs is not one thing. The pilot converged on dense technical reference partly because nothing said otherwise.
values: a getting-started path for someone in a hurry
an exhaustive reference nobody reads end to end
a troubleshooting surface reached in a bad moment
a conceptual explainer arguing for a way of thinking
a changelog that has to carry consequence, not just diffs
a policy and compliance surface with legal weight
a tutorial that has to survive being followed literally
an API reference where the examples matter more than the prose
a migration guide for people who did not want to migrate
